question.text: The function $y_1(x) = e^x$ is a solution to the equation $x y'' - (x+1)y'+ y = 0$ for $x>0.$ Use reduction of order to find a second solution $y_{2}(x)$ to the equation.
question.explanation:
According to the reduction of order method, we let $y_{2}=u(x) \cdot e^x.$

Differentiating $y_{2}=u(x) e^x$ with respect to $x$ gives

\begin{align*} y_{2}' &=u'e^x + u e^x\\[3pt] y_{2}''&=u''e^x + 2u' e^x + ue^x . \end{align*}

Substituting the above into the differential equation gives

\begin{align*} x\left( u''e^x + 2u' e^x + ue^x \right)- (x+1)\left( u'e^x + u e^x \right) + ue^x&=0\\[3pt] e^x\left(u''x + 2u'x + ux\right) - e^xu'(x+1) - e^xu(x+1) + e^xu&=0\\[3pt] e^x\left(u''x + 2u'x + ux - u'(x+1) - u(x+1) + u\right)&=0\\[3pt] e^x\left(u''x + u'(2x-x-1) + u(x-x-1+1) \right)&=0 \\[3pt] e^x\left(u''x + u'(x-1) \right)&=0. \end{align*}

Since $e^x\neq 0,$ we must have

\[ u'' x + u'(x-1) = 0. \]

Let $w=u'.$ Then our equation becomes

\[ w' x + w(x-1)=0. \]

This is a separable equation that has the solution

\[ w = c_1xe^{-x}. \]

But since $w = u',$ we have

\[ u' = c_1 xe^{-x} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad u = - c_1 (1+x)e^{-x} + c_2. \]

Therefore, our expression for $y_2(x) = ue^x$ becomes

\[ y_2(x) = e^x \left(- c_1 (1+x)e^{-x} + c_2\right). \]

Finally, setting $c_1 = -1$ and $c_2 = 0,$ we get

\[ y_2(x) = (1+x). \]

example.title: Finding a Second Solution to a Differential Equation Using Reduction of Order

question.text: Given the function $f(x,y,z) = e^{2x}-y^2z$, find the equation of the tangent plane to the level surface that passes through the point where $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,e^2).$
question.explanation:
The equation of the tangent plane to the level surface $f(x,y,z) = k$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ can be expressed as

\[ \nabla f(x_0,y_0,z_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0, \: z-z_0 \rangle = 0. \]

First, we find the gradient of $f(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at $(x_0,y_0,z_0) = (1,-1,e^2)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \nabla\! f(x,y,z) &= f_x(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{i} + f_y(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{j} + f_z(x,y,z) \, \mathbf{k} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {\partial}{\partial x} (e^{2x}-y^2z) \ \mathbf i + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial y} (e^{2x}-y^2z) \ \mathbf j + \dfrac {\partial}{\partial z} (e^{2x}-y^2z) \ \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= 2e^{2x} \ \mathbf i -2yz \ \mathbf j - y^2 \mathbf k \\[10pt] \nabla\! f(1,-1,e^2) &= 2e^2 \ \mathbf i -2(-1)(e^2) \ \mathbf j - (-1)^2\mathbf k \\[5pt] &= 2e^2 \, \mathbf i + 2e^2 \, \mathbf j - \mathbf k \\[5pt] &= \langle 2e^2, 2e^2, -1 \rangle \end{align*}

We can now write down the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the level surface, as follows:

\begin{align*} \nabla f(x_0,y_0,z_0) \cdot \langle x-x_0, \: y-y_0, \: z-z_0 \rangle & = 0 \\[3pt] \nabla f(1,-1,e^2) \cdot \langle x-1, \: y+1, \: z-e^2 \rangle & = 0 \\[3pt] \langle 2e^2, 2e^2, -1 \rangle \cdot \langle x-1, \: y+1, \: z-e^2 \rangle & = 0 \\[3pt] %e(x-1)+e(y-1)-(z-e) & = 0 \\[3pt] %ex + ey - z - e & = 0 \end{align*}

example.title: Finding the Tangent to Plane a Level Surface

question.text:
\[ \mathcal{B}=\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}, \qquad [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{S}}=\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \]

The basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}$ are given above. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$
question.explanation:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

\[ [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{S}} . \]

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{S}$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}.$ As a result, we have

\[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ -2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}}$ from $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}}\mathbin{:}$

\[\begin{align*} P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}}^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ -2 & -1 \end{bmatrix} ^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {1}{2 \cdot (-1) - (-2) \cdot 2 }\begin{bmatrix} -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{2} & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}\]

Finally, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{S}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{2} & -1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

topic.name: Changing a Basis Using the Change-of-Coordinates Matrix

question.text: Find the shortest distance between the point $P(-2 , -8 , -1)$ and the plane $\Pi$ with equation $2x+y-2z = -7.$
question.explanation:
Let's start by picking a point on the plane. To do that, we simply substitute some concrete values for $x$ and $y$ into the equation and solve for $z.$ Let's choose $x=1$ and $y=-3$ (though it doesn't really matter what values we choose). Solving for $z,$ we get

\begin{align*} 2x+y-2z &= -7 \\[3pt] 2(1)+(-3)+7 &= 2z \\[3pt] 6 &= 2z \\[3pt] z &= 3. \end{align*}

So, we get the point $Q(1 , -3 , 3)$ which lies on the plane.

Computing $\overrightarrow{PQ},$ we get

\begin{align*} \overrightarrow{PQ} &= \langle 1 , -3 , 3 \rangle - \langle -2 , -8 , -1 \rangle \\[3pt] &= \langle 3 , 5 , 4 \rangle. \end{align*}

We also need a normal vector to the plane. For any Cartesian equation of a plane $ax+by+cz=d,$ the normal vector is $\mathbf{n}=\langle a,b,c \rangle.$ So, for the plane $\Pi,$ we have $\mathbf{n}= \langle 2, 1, -2 \rangle.$

Finally, the shortest distance from the point $P$ to the plane $\Pi$ is the absolute value of the scalar projection of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ onto the normal vector of the plane:

\begin{align*} d &= | \text{comp}_{\mathbf{n}} \, \overrightarrow{PQ} | \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{| \overrightarrow{PQ} \cdot \mathbf{n} |}{|\mathbf{n}|} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{| 3 \cdot 2+ 5 \cdot 1+4 \cdot (-2) |}{\sqrt{2^2+1^2+(-2)^2}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{|6+5-8|}{\sqrt{4+1+4}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{|\,3\,|}{\sqrt{9}} \\[5pt] &= 1 \end{align*}

topic.name: The Shortest Distance Between a Plane and a Point

question.text:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $\mathbf{T},$ where $\mathbf T$ is defined as

\[ \mathbf{T}: \begin{bmatrix} u\\v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} v(u-1)^2\\vu^2 \end{bmatrix}. \]
question.choice1: The critical points lie on the lines $u=0, $ $u=1, $ and $v=0.$
question.choice2: The critical points lie on the lines $u=v $ and $v=0.$
question.choice3: The critical points lie on the lines $u=0, $ and $v=u.$
question.choice4: The critical points lie on the lines $u=0, $ and $u=-v.$
question.choice5: The critical points lie on the lines $u=v, $ and $u=-v.$
question.explanation:
Given a transformation

\[ \mathbf{T}:\begin{bmatrix}u\\v\end{bmatrix} \to \begin{bmatrix}x(u,v)\\y(u,v)\end{bmatrix}, \]

the Jacobian determinant of $\mathbf T,$ denoted $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} ,$ is given by

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

To find the locations of the critical points of $\mathbf T,$ we need to solve \[ \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} = 0. \]

Here, we have $x(u,v) = v(u-1)^2$ and $y(u,v) = vu^2.$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} &= 2(u-1)v & \qquad \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} &= (u-1)^2 \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} &= 2uv & \qquad \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} &= u^2 \end{align*}

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} & = \begin{vmatrix} \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial x}{\partial v} \\ \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial u} & \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial v} \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] & = \begin{vmatrix} 2(u-1)v & (u-1)^2 \\ 2uv & u^2 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 2(u-1)v \cdot u^2 - (u-1)^2 \cdot 2uv \\[5pt] &= 2u^2(u-1)v - 2u(u-1)^2v. \end{align*}

The function has critical points when $\dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} =0.$ So, we obtain

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial (x, y)}{\partial (u, v)} &= 0 \\[5pt] 2u^2(u-1)v - 2u(u-1)^2v &= 0 \\[5pt] 2u(u-1)v \left(u-(u-1) \right)&= 0 \\[5pt] 2u(u-1)v&=0. \end{align*}

The equation $2u(u-1)v=0 $ defines the lines $u=0, $ $u=1, $ and $v=0$ in the $uv$-plane.

example.title: Determining the Critical Points of a Transformation

question.text: Given that $ A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 3 & 2 \\ 4 & -10 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} $ has the LU decomposition $A=LU,$ then $l_{21}\cdot u_{23}=$
question.explanation:
To find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we reduce the matrix $A$ to row echelon form. Whilst doing this, we simultaneously write down the row operations applied to $A$ in terms of matrix multiplication using elementary matrices.

\[ \begin{align*} A &= \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 3 & 2 \\ 4 & -10 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} & R_2 &:= R_2 + 4R_1 & \Longleftrightarrow & \qquad \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}^{E_1} \cdot A \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= U \end{align*}\]

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

\begin{align*} E_1 A &= U \\[1ex] A &= E_1^{-1} U \\[1ex] A &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} U \\[1ex] A &= \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} }_{L} \underbrace{ \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix} }_{U} \end{align*}

Therefore, $l_{21}=-4, u_{23}=3,$ and $l_{21}\cdot u_{23}=-12.$

example.title: Finding the LU Factorization Using a Single Elementary Row Operation
